bio.title: The human behind the code
bio.p1: Passionate about computer science since a young age, I've always sought to understand how things work behind the screen.
bio.p2: Today, I don't just understand — I build. As a 3rd-year Computer Science student (Data track) at IUT Créteil-Vitry, I combine academic rigor with real-world challenges at Linedata, where I work as an apprentice Support Analyst.
bio.p3: My goal? Join a master's program in computer science to deepen my skills in development, data and artificial intelligence, and ultimately build solutions that combine technical rigor with real business impact.

aerowise.title: AeroWise — Wildlife risk mapping and analysis
aerowise.subtitle: Search, mapping and AI assistance around airports
aerowise.description: ETL pipeline, API and map interface on a single PostgreSQL stack, with a natural-language assistant.
aerowise.tags: Python, FastAPI, PostgreSQL 16, PostGIS, pgvector, React, deck.gl, Docker
aerowise.context: A final-year university project: cross-referencing species observation data with airport geography to assess a risk, map it, and make it queryable in natural language. The project was rebuilt from scratch after a first version whose architecture proved too heavy to maintain.
aerowise.role: Designing the architecture and building the whole chain: ingestion and transformation scripts, API, data model and assistant integration.
choices: Replacing a three-database architecture — PostgreSQL, Neo4j and Qdrant — with a single PostgreSQL 16 stack using PostGIS, pgvector and pg_trgm. Fewer moving parts, one consistency boundary.
Splitting the ETL into numbered, idempotent scripts so any step can be replayed without starting over or duplicating data.
Giving the AI agent a read-only SQL tool rather than free access to the database.
Making the language model backend configurable through environment variables.
Filtering hexagonal data client-side with deck.gl so interface sliders react instantly.
aerowise.difficulties: The difficulties were operational rather than conceptual: port conflicts between containers, authentication errors on the observation data API, and above all a decimal separator issue on CSV import that silently corrupted coordinates without raising an error. The data loaded, the application ran, and the result was wrong.
aerowise.results: Ten idempotent ETL scripts, nine validated API routes and three interface views: search, risk map and assistant, all deployed with Docker. In hindsight the main contribution is not the AI assistant but the architectural simplification: the second version does the same job with a third of the components.

linedata.title: Financial software maintenance — Linedata
linedata.subtitle: Apprenticeship — support analyst, Lending & Leasing division
linedata.description: Diagnosing and fixing defects in a lending and leasing platform used by banks and leasing companies.
linedata.tags: Java, XML, PL/SQL, Oracle, Drools, GitLab, Unix
linedata.context: The product manages leasing and financing contracts end to end. It ships as a standard core plus one branch per client. My department handles everything that happens after go-live: client-reported defects, small enhancements and data remediation.
linedata.role: Support analyst. I receive incident tickets, reproduce the fault on the client environment, decide whether it affects one client or all of them, find the cause, fix, test and document the work through to closure.
choices: Diagnosing by successive elimination rather than reading code linearly — on a twenty-year-old codebase, it is the only approach that converges.
Using version history as a source of knowledge: who changed a file, when and for which ticket, in the absence of complete technical documentation.
Always separating the fix for the cause from the repair of already-damaged data, which requires a remediation script tested beforehand.
linedata.difficulties: The sheer size of the code, written over two decades by dozens of people. The business dimension: without understanding residual value or payment schedules, a defect is unreadable. And non-reproducible faults, which force you to reason about environment differences without ever observing the problem.
linedata.results: Twenty tickets handled over the period, fourteen closed. One notable case: identifying a framework defect on a search screen where the business rule was correct but evaluated only once, at load time. The deliverable was not a fix but a diagnosis handed to the development team.
traces: Detailed apprenticeship report — available on request
Diagram of the incident handling process

campus.title: Centralised database & dashboard
campus.subtitle: Internship — Campus des entrepreneurs
campus.description: Unifying scattered data into a single database, automated migration and real-time reporting.
campus.context: The organisation kept its data in several separate files with no single source of truth: figures diverged between documents and reports were rebuilt by hand every time.
campus.role: Designing the centralised data model, writing the migration from existing sources, connecting external platforms through APIs, and building the dashboard.
choices: Automating the migration with a script rather than moving data by hand, so it could be replayed as often as needed.
Feeding the database through API calls to external platforms, avoiding re-entry and keeping data fresh.
Automating recurring reports rather than delivering a dashboard alone.
campus.difficulties: Most of the time went into source data quality rather than code: duplicates across files, inconsistent date formats, free-text fields where a controlled list was needed. Every cleaning rule had to be validated with the business user, because what looks like a typo is sometimes a legitimate case.
campus.results: The organisation now has a single source fed automatically, and reports that were rebuilt by hand are produced without intervention. My main takeaway is that the difficulty of a data project rarely lies in the technology — it lies in understanding the business that produced the data.

portfolio.title: This portfolio
portfolio.subtitle: A bilingual web application, designed and deployed end to end
portfolio.description: Personal site in Next.js: localisation, light and dark themes, contact form and continuous deployment.
portfolio.tags: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, next-intl, Framer Motion, Vercel
portfolio.context: This site serves two purposes: showing my work to recruiters, and acting as evidence for the validation of my degree competencies. Those two audiences want different things, which shaped the structure of the site.
portfolio.role: Design, development and deployment, alone, from mockup to production.
choices: Next.js with the App Router and next-intl: all content exists in French and English, each page served in the language of its URL.
Light and dark themes driven by CSS variables rather than two sets of classes, so each colour is defined in one place only.
Structure separated from content: all text lives in translation files, no hard-coded strings in the code.
Continuous deployment on Vercel: every commit on the main branch triggers a build and a release.
portfolio.difficulties: Two things took longer than expected. First, applying the theme on load: without care, the page briefly renders in the wrong theme before the stored preference is read. Second, localised routing: combining a language prefix in the URL, a switch that keeps the current page and static rendering per language requires knowing exactly where next-intl sits in the render cycle.
portfolio.results: A live, bilingual, responsive site, redeployed automatically on every commit. The code is public and is itself evidence for the Build competency — the only project here whose sources the panel can open while I present it.

meteo.title: Weather web application
meteo.subtitle: Coursework — visualising weather measurements
meteo.description: Browsing and charting weather measurements recorded across France.
meteo.tags: Java, PHP, MySQL, JavaScript, Chart.js, HTML/CSS
meteo.context: A university assignment: making a set of weather records usable through a browsing interface and graphical representations.
meteo.role: Building the whole application: data model and queries, processing layer, then the browsing interface and charts.
choices: MVC architecture, separating data access, processing logic and display.
Chart.js on the client for rendering, keeping the server focused on serving data.
meteo.difficulties: Data volume was the main obstacle: early aggregation queries became too slow for comfortable display. The subtler issue was missing values — not every station records every measurement, and a chart built without handling those gaps looks right but is not.
meteo.results: The application lets you browse measurements by station and period and compare them graphically. In hindsight it is the first project where I understood that a correct display depends first on the quality of the data model behind it.

Competences.heading: My
Competences.subtitle: The six competencies of the BUT in Computer Science, data management track, each backed by concrete work.
Competences.disclaimer: Level 3 statements are taken from the national framework of the data management track.

realiser.name: Build an application
realiser.statement: Adapt applications across a range of platforms
realiser.covers: Design, code, test and integrate a software solution, then keep it running across different platforms and execution contexts.
realiser.self: Achieved first through adapting existing software: reading code I did not write, understanding its conventions and changing it without breaking the rest. This portfolio covered the other side — designing from scratch, choosing an architecture and shipping it.

evidence.text: This site, built end to end: Next.js, French and English localisation, light and dark themes, responsive from mobile to desktop.
Java and XML fixes on a product shipped in as many variants as it has clients, with the conventions and regression constraints that implies.
A complete web application in MVC architecture, with graphical rendering of measurements.

optimiser.name: Optimise applications
optimiser.statement: Select the right algorithms for a given problem
optimiser.covers: Choose and tune processing against measurable criteria: execution time, accuracy, resource use.
optimiser.self: My practice rests on two things: tracing a root cause by elimination, and choosing the right storage structure for each kind of data. Rebuilding AeroWise is the clearest example: three separate databases replaced by one, with no loss of functionality.

evidence.text: Hybrid storage chosen per data type, and model selection driven by the task rather than one pipeline for every case.
Fault diagnosis by successive elimination of hypotheses on a codebase over twenty years old.

administrer.name: Administer complex networked systems
administrer.statement: Deploy services within a network architecture
administrer.covers: Install, configure, deploy and keep services, infrastructure and runtime environments operational.
administrer.self: Achieved through daily practice: standing up a full application environment locally, connecting to remote machines, reading logs, containerising and deploying. Sizing an infrastructure is the next step, and so far I have only approached it in theory.

evidence.text: Local application environments on Tomcat or JBoss depending on the client, remote Unix machines, log analysis and debug execution.
Continuous deployment: every commit on the main branch triggers a build and a release on Vercel.

gerer.name: Manage information and data
gerer.statement: Administer a database, design and build decision-support systems
gerer.covers: Design a data model, administer it, guarantee its consistency and turn it into information usable for decision-making.
gerer.self: The core of my track and the competency I have most material on. The apprenticeship added the production dimension: real data accumulated over twenty years, with irreversible operations. I learned to separate fixing a defect's cause from repairing the data it has already damaged.

evidence.text: A centralised database built from scattered sources, automated migration and a real-time dashboard.
Consistency analysis on a production table, then a PL/SQL remediation script written and tested to restore missing balances.
Modelling heterogeneous data — geospatial, relational and vector — each in the appropriate store.

conduire.name: Run a project
conduire.statement: Take part in designing and delivering an information-system project
conduire.covers: Frame a need, organise the work, meet deadlines and report on progress.
conduire.self: Achieved across three complementary settings: a university team project from framing to final demo, an internship assignment delivered to a non-technical stakeholder, and a portfolio of prioritised tickets in a company — where I controlled neither the arrival nor the deadline.

evidence.text: A university team project, from framing the need to the final demonstration.
An internship assignment run from requirements gathering to delivery, with a non-technical stakeholder.
A portfolio of twenty tickets prioritised by severity, some spanning several months.

collaborer.name: Work within a software team
collaborer.covers: Fit into an organisation, communicate with people from different disciplines, and eventually lead.
collaborer.self: Achieved in a team where you work alone on a ticket but never alone on a problem: knowing who to take a subject to, phrasing a workable request for help, adjusting how you explain things to your audience. On university projects I handled task allocation and integration of contributions. Leading an established team is the next step.

evidence.text: Daily work with first-line support, product experts, the development team and the systems team; every change reviewed by a peer through a merge request.
Sharing out the work and integrating contributions within a project team.
